[Ben Sasse on Faith, Family, and Facing Death](https://www.econtalk.org/ben-sasse-on-faith-family-and-facing-death/),
EconTalk, 10 August 2026.

Ben Sasse, the former senator and University of Florida president, talks with
Russ Roberts six months into a stage-four pancreatic cancer diagnosis that had
given him 90 days. He talks about faith and mortality, about workaholism as an
idol his illness broke, and about his marriage.

## Concerts, Sporting Events and Worship

**Near the end, Roberts asks whether concerts and sporting events have taken
the place of church.** Religion is in decline in the West, he says, yet at a
Bruce Springsteen concert the crowd treats Springsteen "like a god", and at the
World Cup "tens of thousands of Scots" sing "The Flower of
Scotland". He reads both as "the same impulse to be part of something larger
than yourself with a group of other people", without the theology.

**Sasse answers that people always worship something, so the question is
what.** "Functionally, humans are always worshiping something. Money, sex,
power, fame, me, me, me." Singing together is close to the centre of Christian
practice: of the four marks of a Christian in Paul's letter to the Ephesians,
"two of the four are *singing*", and a third, gratitude, is the impulse to
sing.

**Sasse distinguishes between crowds by where they point the feeling.**

- **The mob** "is a danger that should always be resisted".
- **A football game** is tribal, and he allows it: "I understand the
  Aristotelian catharsis that happens in tribe around a football game."
- **Springsteen** draws the crowd's feeling to himself. The show "does feel
  self-referential", and the political speeches land as an anticlimax.
- **Alan Jackson** gives the feeling back to the audience: "he turns that
  nostalgic impulse toward a communal event back on people so that their
  experience can go with him".

## Do Not Go Gentle into That Good Night

Roberts closes by reading Dylan Thomas's "Do not go gentle into that good
night". He describes Sasse as "a man who tries to walk with your head bowed
down while you still rage against the dying of the light", fighting the cancer
while accepting it. Sasse answers that he can't beat that poem, and that
"there is a wisdom in numbering our days", the line from Psalm 90.
